name: Cannabis use disorder
summary: No medication is FDA-approved for cannabis use disorder or cannabis withdrawal. Psychosocial treatments (CBT, motivational enhancement, contingency management) are first-line. Pharmacotherapy evidence is limited and mixed (Cochrane 2019). Investigational agents such as AEF0117 and PP-01 remain in clinical trials.
plainSummary: Cannabis use disorder means having trouble cutting back on marijuana even when it causes problems. No medicine is approved for it, so counseling is the main treatment; a few medicines are being studied.
noApprovedNote: No FDA-approved medication exists for cannabis use disorder or cannabis withdrawal as of October 2026. Searches for 2024–2026 FDA approvals found none; candidates such as AEF0117 and PP-01 are still investigational. All options below are off-label with limited evidence.

offLabel.use: Reduce cannabis use and withdrawal symptoms (sleep, craving)
offLabel.notes: A small 12-week proof-of-concept RCT (1200 mg/day) found reduced use and withdrawal symptoms, but it has not been replicated in large trials. Cautions: sedation, misuse potential (especially with opioids), and renal dosing.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for postherpetic neuralgia and adjunctive partial-onset seizures; not for cannabis use disorder.

dosing.target: 1,200 mg/day in divided doses (the 12-week trial dose)
dosing.max: 1,200 mg/day in the trial (labeled seizure maximum 3,600 mg/day)
dosing.notes: Titrate to tolerability; reduce for renal impairment.

warnings: Respiratory depression with opioids or other CNS depressants
details.plainSummary: A nerve-pain and seizure medicine that reduced cannabis use and withdrawal symptoms in a small trial. Larger trials have not confirmed it.

references.label: Mason BJ, et al. A proof-of-concept randomized controlled study of gabapentin in cannabis dependence. Neuropsychopharmacology 2012
Nielsen S, et al. Pharmacotherapies for cannabis dependence. Cochrane 2019

offLabel.use: Adjunct to contingency management, mainly studied in adolescents
offLabel.notes: A 2012 adolescent RCT (1200 mg twice daily) doubled the odds of negative urine tests, but a large adult trial and a 2025 youth trial did not confirm benefit. Generally well tolerated (GI upset).

details.labeledFor: Dietary supplement in the US; prescription acetylcysteine is FDA-approved for acetaminophen overdose and as a mucolytic. Not for cannabis use disorder.

dosing.target: 2,400 mg/day (1,200 mg twice daily, adolescent trial)
dosing.notes: Added to contingency management in the positive adolescent trial; adult and later youth trials were negative.

formulations: Prescription oral solution and IV (other indications)
warnings: GI upset, nausea, and sulfur odor
Bronchospasm in people with asthma (inhaled form)
details.plainSummary: An over-the-counter supplement studied to cut cannabis use in teens. Results were mixed.

references.label: Gray KM, et al. N-acetylcysteine in cannabis-dependent adolescents. Am J Psychiatry 2012
N-acetylcysteine for youth cannabis use disorder: randomized controlled trial main findings. Neuropsychopharmacology 2025

offLabel.notes: A 2019 Cochrane review found that THC preparations (including nabiximols, not available in the US) may reduce withdrawal and improve retention but do not clearly increase abstinence. Cautions: dronabinol is C-III and nabilone C-II; sedation, psychoactive effects, and misuse potential.

details.labeledFor: Dronabinol (Marinol, Syndros) is FDA-approved for chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting and AIDS-related anorexia; nabilone (Cesamet) for chemotherapy nausea/vomiting. Not for cannabis withdrawal.

dosing.start: Dronabinol 2.5–5 mg twice daily; nabilone 0.5–1 mg at bedtime
dosing.target: Dronabinol up to about 20 mg twice daily in trials; nabilone about 6 mg/day in a small study
dosing.max: Dronabinol 40 mg/day and nabilone 6 mg/day (trial maxima)
dosing.notes: Supervised use in specialty programs; avoid driving.

formulations: Dronabinol capsules 2.5, 5, 10 mg; oral solution 5 mg/mL
contraindications: Dronabinol capsules: hypersensitivity to dronabinol or sesame oil
Dronabinol solution: disulfiram or metronidazole use (contains alcohol)
details.plainSummary: Lab-made THC medicines that may ease cannabis withdrawal but do not clearly help people stop. They can cause sleepiness and a high.

references.label: Nielsen S, et al. Pharmacotherapies for cannabis dependence. Cochrane 2019

offLabel.notes: A 2026 phase 2 RCT (n=174) found no effect overall, with reduced use in men but not women. Evidence is insufficient to support routine use. Cautions: nausea and abnormal dreams. May be reasonable to consider when tobacco is co-used.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved as an aid to smoking cessation; not for cannabis use disorder.

dosing.start: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days
dosing.max: 2 mg/day; 0.5 mg twice daily at most if CrCl below 30 mL/min
dosing.notes: Take with food and water to limit nausea.

contraindications: Serious hypersensitivity or skin reactions to varenicline
warnings: Seizures (rare); cardiovascular events in people with heart disease
details.plainSummary: A stop-smoking medicine that did not reduce cannabis use overall in a recent trial. It might be considered when tobacco is also used.

references.label: McRae-Clark AL, et al. Varenicline for cannabis use disorder: a randomized controlled trial. Addiction 2026
